title: Grade 8 Square Roots and Real Numbers
seo_title: Grade 8 Square Roots and Real Numbers Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Estimate and calculate square roots, in various contexts
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 math worksheets on square roots and real numbers for the Ontario curriculum: perfect squares, estimating square roots, rational and irrational numbers, ordering numbers like √10, π and 3.2, and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: √50 is between 7 and 8, because 7² = 49 and 8² = 64. It is about 7.1, not 25.
key_sub: The square root of a whole number that is not a perfect square is irrational. π is irrational too: 3.14 is only close to it.
body_html:
Perfect squares and square roots

A perfect square is a whole number times itself: 7 × 7 = 49, so 49 is a perfect square. The square root undoes squaring. √49 = 7, because 72 = 49.

n1011121314152030
n2100121144169196225400900

Decimals and fractions can have exact roots too: √0.49 = 0.7 and √916 = 34.

Estimating a square root

Find the perfect squares on each side of the number. The root is between their roots.

Example 1

Estimate √30 to one decimal place.

52 = 25 and 62 = 36, so √30 is between 5 and 6, a little closer to 5. Try 5.42 = 29.16 and 5.52 = 30.25. 30 is closer to 30.25.

Answer: √30 ≈ 5.5

Rational and irrational numbers

A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers. Its decimal stops (0.75) or repeats (0.3 = 13). An irrational number cannot be written as a fraction. Its decimal never ends and never repeats.

RationalIrrational
−5, 0.75, 0.3, 227, √49 = 7π, √2, √10, √50, 0.1010010001…

Together, the rational and irrational numbers make the real numbers. The square root of a whole number that is not a perfect square is always irrational.

Ordering real numbers

Change each number to a decimal, then compare.

Example 2

A square field has an area of 2500 m2. How long is each side?

Side × side = 2500. 50 × 50 = 2500.

Answer: 50 m

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
√50 ≈ 25Do not halve. 72 = 49, so √50 ≈ 7.1
π is rational, because π = 3.143.14 is only close to π. π never ends or repeats, so it is irrational
Every square root is irrational√49 = 7 and √0.25 = 0.5 are rational
√0.49 = 0.070.07 × 0.07 = 0.0049. √0.49 = 0.7
√36 + √64 = √100 = 10Find each root first: 6 + 8 = 14

faq.q: How do you estimate a square root without a calculator?
faq.a: Find the perfect squares on each side of the number. For √50: 7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64, so √50 is between 7 and 8 and very close to 7, about 7.1.

faq.q: Is π a rational or irrational number?
faq.a: π is irrational. Its decimal 3.14159… never ends and never repeats. 3.14 and 22/7 are rational numbers that are only close to π.

faq.q: Which Ontario Grade 8 expectations cover square roots and real numbers?
faq.a: In the Number strand of the 2020 Ontario math curriculum, B1.3 is about estimating and calculating square roots, B1.2 about rational and irrational numbers, and B2.2 about perfect squares and square roots.

faq.q: What are the perfect squares from 1 to 400?

items.q: What is √49?
What is √81?
What is √121?
What is √144?
What is √225?
What is √400?
What is √900?
What is 13<sup>2</sup>?
What is 16<sup>2</sup>?
Which number is a perfect square?
items.e: 196 = 14 × 14, so 196 is a perfect square. 160, 140 and 200 are not: 122 = 144, 132 = 169, 142 = 196 and 152 = 225. A number ending in 0 is not always a square.

items.q: Which number is a perfect square?
items.e: 225 = 15 × 15, so 225 is a perfect square. 125 = 5 × 5 × 5 is a cube, not a square. 250 and 150 are between perfect squares.

items.q: Which number is not a perfect square?
items.e: 36 = 62, 64 = 82 and 100 = 102. 92 = 81 and 102 = 100, so 90 is not a perfect square, even though 9 is a perfect square.

items.q: What is √0.49?
What is √0.09?
What is √1.44?
What is √916?
items.e: Take the square root of the top and the bottom: √9 = 3 and √16 = 4, so √916 = 34. Check: 34 × 34 = 916.

items.q: What is √2536?
items.e: Take the square root of the top and the bottom: √25 = 5 and √36 = 6, so √2536 = 56. Check: 56 × 56 = 2536.

items.q: The area of this square is 64 cm2. How long is each side?
items.e: The area of a square is side × side. 8 × 8 = 64, so each side is √64 = 8 cm. Dividing by 4 (16) gives the side from the perimeter, not the area.

items.q: The area of this square is 169 m2. How long is each side?
items.e: The area of a square is side × side. 13 × 13 = 169, so each side is √169 = 13 m. Dividing by 4 (42.25) gives the side from the perimeter, not the area.

items.q: What is √36 + √64?
items.e: Find each root first: √36 = 6 and √64 = 8, so √36 + √64 = 6 + 8 = 14. You cannot add under the root sign: √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 is a different number.

items.q: √50 is between which two whole numbers?
items.e: Find the perfect squares on each side: 72 = 49 and 82 = 64. 50 is between them, so √50 is between 7 and 8. (√50 is about 7.07.)

items.q: √30 is between which two whole numbers?
items.e: Find the perfect squares on each side: 52 = 25 and 62 = 36. 30 is between them, so √30 is between 5 and 6. (√30 is about 5.48.)

items.q: √20 is between which two whole numbers?
items.e: Find the perfect squares on each side: 42 = 16 and 52 = 25. 20 is between them, so √20 is between 4 and 5. (√20 is about 4.47.)

items.q: √75 is between which two whole numbers?
items.e: Find the perfect squares on each side: 82 = 64 and 92 = 81. 75 is between them, so √75 is between 8 and 9. (√75 is about 8.66.)

items.q: √90 is between which two whole numbers?
items.e: Find the perfect squares on each side: 92 = 81 and 102 = 100. 90 is between them, so √90 is between 9 and 10. (√90 is about 9.49.)

items.q: √110 is between which two whole numbers?
items.e: Find the perfect squares on each side: 102 = 100 and 112 = 121. 110 is between them, so √110 is between 10 and 11. (√110 is about 10.49.)

items.q: √130 is between which two whole numbers?
items.e: Find the perfect squares on each side: 112 = 121 and 122 = 144. 130 is between them, so √130 is between 11 and 12. (√130 is about 11.40.)

items.q: √200 is between which two whole numbers?
items.e: Find the perfect squares on each side: 142 = 196 and 152 = 225. 200 is between them, so √200 is between 14 and 15. (√200 is about 14.14.)

items.q: Which point is closest to √40 on the number line?
items.e: 62 = 36 and 72 = 49, so √40 is between 6 and 7. 40 is closer to 36, so √40 is closer to 6. √40 ≈ 6.32, so the answer is point C.

items.q: Which point is closest to √80 on the number line?
items.e: 82 = 64 and 92 = 81, so √80 is between 8 and 9. 80 is closer to 81, so √80 is closer to 9. √80 ≈ 8.94, so the answer is point D.

items.q: Which point is closest to √10 on the number line?
items.e: 32 = 9 and 42 = 16, so √10 is between 3 and 4. 10 is closer to 9, so √10 is closer to 3. √10 ≈ 3.16, so the answer is point B.

items.q: Which point is closest to √55 on the number line?
items.e: 72 = 49 and 82 = 64, so √55 is between 7 and 8. 55 is closer to 49, so √55 is closer to 7. √55 ≈ 7.42, so the answer is point C.

items.q: Which whole number is √60 closest to?
items.e: 72 = 49 and 82 = 64. 60 is closer to 64, so √60 is closest to 8. (√60 ≈ 7.75.) The answer is a root, not the perfect square 64.

items.q: Which whole number is √28 closest to?
items.e: 52 = 25 and 62 = 36. 28 is closer to 25, so √28 is closest to 5. (√28 ≈ 5.29.) The answer is a root, not the perfect square 25.

items.q: Which whole number is √84 closest to?
items.e: 92 = 81 and 102 = 100. 84 is closer to 81, so √84 is closest to 9. (√84 ≈ 9.17.) The answer is a root, not the perfect square 81.

items.q: Which whole number is √140 closest to?
items.e: 112 = 121 and 122 = 144. 140 is closer to 144, so √140 is closest to 12. (√140 ≈ 11.83.) The answer is a root, not the perfect square 144.

items.q: Estimate √50 to one decimal place.
items.e: 72 = 49 and 82 = 64, so √50 is between 7 and 8. √50 ≈ 7.071, so to one decimal place √50 ≈ 7.1. Check: 7.12 = 50.41, close to 50.

items.q: Estimate √22 to one decimal place.
items.e: 42 = 16 and 52 = 25, so √22 is between 4 and 5. √22 ≈ 4.690, so to one decimal place √22 ≈ 4.7. Check: 4.72 = 22.09, close to 22.

items.q: Estimate √45 to one decimal place.
items.e: 62 = 36 and 72 = 49, so √45 is between 6 and 7. √45 ≈ 6.708, so to one decimal place √45 ≈ 6.7. Check: 6.72 = 44.89, close to 45.

items.q: Estimate √88 to one decimal place.
items.e: 92 = 81 and 102 = 100, so √88 is between 9 and 10. √88 ≈ 9.381, so to one decimal place √88 ≈ 9.4. Check: 9.42 = 88.36, close to 88.

items.q: Is √49 rational or irrational?
c: Irrational, because every square root is irrational
Irrational, because 49 is not a perfect square
items.e: 7 × 7 = 49, so √49 = 7, and 7 = 71 is rational. The square root of a perfect square is rational.

items.q: Is √12 rational or irrational?
c: Irrational, because 12 is not a perfect square
Rational, because 12 is a whole number
items.e: 9 < 12 < 16, so 12 is not a perfect square. Its root, 3.4641…, never ends and never repeats, so √12 is irrational.

items.q: Is π rational or irrational?
c: Rational, because π = 227
Irrational, because its decimal never ends or repeats
items.e: π = 3.14159265… never ends and never repeats, so π is irrational. 3.14 and 227 are only close to π.

items.q: Is 0.3 rational or irrational?
c: Irrational, because 3 does not divide 10 evenly
Rational, because it equals 13
Rational, because it equals 310
Irrational, because its decimal never ends
items.e: 1 ÷ 3 = 0.333…, so 0.3 = 13. A repeating decimal is rational. 310 = 0.3 stops after one digit.

items.q: Is −5 rational or irrational?
c: Irrational, because −5 is not a whole number
Irrational, because it is not written as a fraction
items.e: −5 = −51, a quotient of two integers, so it is rational. Every integer is rational.

items.q: Is 227 rational or irrational?
c: Rational, because it is a fraction of two integers
Irrational, because 22 ÷ 7 does not divide evenly
items.e: 227 is 22 ÷ 7, a quotient of two integers, so it is rational. Its decimal 3.142857142857… repeats. It is close to π but not equal to it.

items.q: Is √0.25 rational or irrational?
c: Irrational, because it is the root of a decimal
Irrational, because 0.25 is not a perfect square
items.e: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25, so √0.25 = 0.5 = 12, which is rational. Halving gives 0.125, but 0.125 × 0.125 = 0.015625.

items.q: Is 0.1010010001… rational or irrational?
c: Rational, because the decimal has a pattern
Irrational, because the digits never end and never repeat
Rational, because it only uses the digits 0 and 1
items.e: The number of 0s keeps growing (1, 2, 3, …), so no block of digits repeats. The decimal never ends and never repeats: it is irrational.

items.q: Which number is irrational?
items.e: 16 is a perfect square (√16 = 4), but 20 is not. So √20 = 4.472… is irrational. 0.25 and 45 are rational.

items.q: Which number is irrational?
items.e: π = 3.14159… never ends and never repeats. 3.14 and 227 are fractions close to π, and √9 = 3.

items.q: Which number is irrational?
items.e: In 0.1211211121112… the number of 1s keeps growing, so no block repeats. 0.12 repeats 12, so it is rational (433).

items.q: Which number is irrational?
items.e: √0.04 = 0.2, √49 = 23 and −√64 = −8 are rational. 50 is not a perfect square, so √50 is irrational.

items.q: Which number is rational?
items.e: 6 × 6 = 36, so √36 = 6 is rational. 6 and 30 are not perfect squares, and π is irrational.

items.q: Which number is rational?
items.e: 0.4 = 0.444… repeats, so it is rational: it equals 49. The other decimals never end and never repeat.

items.q: Which number is rational?
items.e: −73 is a quotient of two integers, so it is rational, even though it is negative. 2π, √11 and √7 are irrational.

items.q: Which number is rational?
items.e: 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21, so √1.21 = 1.1 is rational. 1.2, 12 and 120 are not perfect squares of rational numbers.

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: Every integer is a rational number.
items.e: Any integer can be written over 1, for example −4 = −41, so every integer is rational. π is irrational, √9 = 3 is rational, and repeating decimals are rational.

items.q: Which statement about √2 is true?
c: It is rational, because 2 is an integer.
Its decimal never ends and never repeats.
items.e: 1.41 × 1.41 = 1.9881, not 2, and no fraction squares to exactly 2. √2 = 1.41421356… never ends and never repeats, so it is irrational.

items.q: Which sets of numbers does −6 belong to?
items.e: Whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, …, so −6 is not one. −6 is an integer, and every integer is a rational number (−61).

items.q: Which fraction is equal to 0.3?
items.e: 1 ÷ 3 = 0.333… with the 3 repeating forever, so 0.3 = 13. 33100 = 0.33 stops after two digits.

items.q: Which number is greater: √10 or 3.2?
items.e: Square the decimal: 3.22 = 10.24, and 10.24 > 10. So 3.2 > √10, and 3.2 is greater. (√10 ≈ 3.162.)

items.q: Which number is greater: √20 or 4.4?
items.e: Square the decimal: 4.42 = 19.36, and 19.36 < 20. So 4.4 < √20, and √20 is greater. (√20 ≈ 4.472.)

items.q: Which number is greater: π or √10?
items.e: π ≈ 3.142 and √10 ≈ 3.162. So √10 is greater, but only by about 0.02.

items.q: Which number is greater: √50 or 7.1?
items.e: Square the decimal: 7.12 = 50.41, and 50.41 > 50. So 7.1 > √50, and 7.1 is greater. (√50 ≈ 7.071.)

items.q: Which number is greater: √30 or 5.5?
items.e: Square the decimal: 5.52 = 30.25, and 30.25 > 30. So 5.5 > √30, and 5.5 is greater. (√30 ≈ 5.477.)

items.q: Which number is greater: √65 or 8.1?
items.e: Square the decimal: 8.12 = 65.61, and 65.61 > 65. So 8.1 > √65, and 8.1 is greater. (√65 ≈ 8.062.)

items.q: Which list is in order from least to greatest: √10, π, 3.2?
items.e: Write each as a decimal: π ≈ 3.142, √10 ≈ 3.162, 3.2. From least to greatest: π, √10, 3.2.

items.q: Which list is in order from least to greatest: √5, 2.2, 94?
items.e: Write each as a decimal: 2.2, √5 ≈ 2.236, 94 = 2.25. From least to greatest: 2.2, √5, 94.

items.q: Which list is in order from least to greatest: √2, 1.4, 1.5?
items.e: Write each as a decimal: 1.4, √2 ≈ 1.414, 1.5. From least to greatest: 1.4, √2, 1.5.

items.q: Which list is in order from least to greatest: √40, 6.3, 2π?
items.e: Write each as a decimal: 2π ≈ 6.283, 6.3, √40 ≈ 6.325. From least to greatest: 2π, 6.3, √40.

items.q: Which list is in order from least to greatest: −√9, −2.5, −√5?
items.e: Write each as a decimal: −√9 = −3, −2.5, −√5 ≈ −2.236. From least to greatest: −√9, −2.5, −√5.

items.q: Which list is in order from least to greatest: √17, 4.1, 174?
items.e: Write each as a decimal: 4.1, √17 ≈ 4.123, 174 = 4.25. From least to greatest: 4.1, √17, 174.

items.q: Which number is between 5 and 6?
items.e: 52 = 25 and 62 = 36, so a square root between 5 and 6 must have a number between 25 and 36 under the root sign. Only √30 works (√30 ≈ 5.48).

items.q: Which number is between 8 and 9?
items.e: 82 = 64 and 92 = 81, so a square root between 8 and 9 must have a number between 64 and 81 under the root sign. Only √70 works (√70 ≈ 8.37).

items.q: Which number is between 3 and 4?
items.e: 32 = 9 and 42 = 16, so a square root between 3 and 4 must have a number between 9 and 16 under the root sign. Only √12 works (√12 ≈ 3.46).

items.q: Which number is the greatest: 5.01, 5.09, 5.1, √26?
items.e: As decimals: 5.01, 5.09, √26 ≈ 5.099, 5.1. The greatest is 5.1.

items.q: Which number is the least: 3.14, 227, π, √10?
items.e: As decimals: 3.14, π ≈ 3.142, 227 ≈ 3.143, √10 ≈ 3.162. The least is 3.14. π is a little more than 3.14, so 3.14 is not equal to π.

items.q: Which number is the greatest: −1.4, −1.5, −√2, −√3?
items.e: As decimals: −√3 ≈ −1.732, −1.5, −√2 ≈ −1.414, −1.4. The greatest is −1.4. For negative numbers, the one closest to 0 is the greatest.

items.q: Which number is the least: 0.5, 0.71, √0.2, √0.5?
Which number is the greatest: 10, 9.9, √101, √99?

sets.title: Word problems: squares, sides and areas

items.q: A square soccer practice field in Mississauga has an area of 2500 m<sup>2</sup>. How long is each side?
items.e: Side × side = 2500. 50 × 50 = 2500, so each side is √2500 = 50 m.

items.q: Kai plants a square vegetable garden with an area of 40 m<sup>2</sup>. Each side is between which two lengths?
items.e: 62 = 36 and 72 = 49. 40 is between them, so each side is between 6 m and 7 m (√40 ≈ 6.32 m).

items.q: A square patio at a cottage has an area of 30 m<sup>2</sup>. How long is each side, to the nearest tenth of a metre?
items.e: √30 ≈ 5.477. The hundredths digit is 7, so round up: 5.5 m. Check: 5.52 = 30.25, which is close to 30.

items.q: A square horse paddock near Guelph has an area of 900 m<sup>2</sup>. How much fencing goes around it?
items.e: Each side is √900 = 30 m. A square has 4 equal sides: 4 × 30 = 120 m.

items.q: For a school assembly, 196 chairs are set out in a square: the number of rows equals the number of chairs in each row. How many rows are there?
items.e: Rows × chairs per row = 196, and they are equal. 14 × 14 = 196, so there are 14 rows.

items.q: Sofia sews a square quilt from 64 small square patches. How many patches are in each row?
items.e: Patches per row × number of rows = 64, and the quilt is square. 8 × 8 = 64, so there are 8 patches in each row.

items.q: An art class in Ottawa paints on a square canvas with an area of 0.81 m<sup>2</sup>. How long is each side?
Maya floods a square backyard rink with an area of 150 m<sup>2</sup>. To the nearest metre, how long is each side?
items.e: 122 = 144 and 132 = 169. 150 is much closer to 144, so the side is about 12 m (√150 ≈ 12.25 m).

items.q: A square bathroom floor has an area of 16 m<sup>2</sup>. It is covered with square tiles that are 0.5 m on each side. How many tiles are in each row?
items.e: Each side of the floor is √16 = 4 m. 4 ÷ 0.5 = 8 tiles in each row (and 64 tiles in all).

items.q: A square farm field near Woodstock has an area of 4 hectares. One hectare is 10 000 m<sup>2</sup>. How long is each side of the field?
items.e: 4 hectares = 4 × 10 000 = 40 000 m2. 200 × 200 = 40 000, so each side is 200 m. √4 = 2 forgets to change hectares to square metres.

items.q: In science class, students learn that the time in seconds for a ball to fall d metres is about √(d ÷ 4.9). A ball is dropped from a balcony 19.6 m high. About how long does it take to reach the ground?
items.e: 19.6 ÷ 4.9 = 4, and √4 = 2 seconds. Do not stop at 4: you still need the square root.

items.q: Liam has a square tablecloth with an area of 2 m<sup>2</sup>. Is it wide enough to cover a square table that is 1.5 m wide?
c: No. Each side is about 1.4 m.
items.e: Each side is √2 ≈ 1.41 m, and 1.41 < 1.5. No, it is about 9 cm too narrow. √2 is not 2: 2 × 2 = 4.

items.q: A square poster for the Terry Fox Run has an area of 3600 cm<sup>2</sup>. How long is each side?

Noah has a square photo with an area of 100 cm<sup>2</sup>. He wants a square print with double the area, 200 cm<sup>2</sup>. To the nearest tenth of a centimetre, how long is each side of the new print?
items.e: Each side is √200 ≈ 14.142 cm ≈ 14.1 cm. Doubling the side to 20 cm would make the area 400 cm2, four times as big.

items.q: A tent for a canoe trip in Algonquin Park has a square floor with an area of 6.25 m<sup>2</sup>. How long is each side?
A square cottage lot has an area of 1000 m<sup>2</sup>. Each side is between which two lengths?
items.e: 312 = 961 and 322 = 1024. 1000 is between them, so each side is between 31 m and 32 m (√1000 ≈ 31.62 m).

items.q: A square has an area of 50 cm<sup>2</sup>. Ethan says each side is 25 cm. Which statement is correct?
c: Ethan is wrong. Each side is about 7.1 cm.
Ethan is wrong. Each side is 12.5 cm.
Ethan is wrong. Each side is about 7.5 cm.
items.e: 25 × 25 = 625, not 50. 72 = 49, so √50 is just over 7: √50 ≈ 7.07 ≈ 7.1 cm. 12.5 is 50 ÷ 4, the side from a perimeter of 50 cm.

items.q: Emma builds a square sandbox with an area of 5 m<sup>2</sup>. She has 9 m of wood for the border. Is that enough?
items.e: Each side is √5 ≈ 2.236 m. The border is 4 × 2.236 ≈ 8.94 m, which is less than 9 m. Yes, it is enough. (4 × 5 = 20 uses the area as the side.)

items.q: A square sheet of plywood for a snow fort roof has an area of 2.89 m<sup>2</sup>. How long is each side?
items.e: 1.7 × 1.7 = 2.89, so each side is √2.89 = 1.7 m. Check the decimal place: 17 × 17 = 289, and 2.89 has two decimal places, so the root has one.

items.q: Plot A in a community garden is a square with an area of 50 m<sup>2</sup>. Plot B is a square with sides of 7.2 m. Which plot has longer sides?
c: Plot A, because 50 is greater than 7.2
They have the same side length
items.e: Plot A’s side is √50 ≈ 7.07 m. 7.07 < 7.2, so Plot B has longer sides. Compare side with side, not area with side.
